'''Sandra J. Rosenthal''' (born 1966) is the Jack and Pamela Egan Professor of Chemistry, professor of physics and astronomy, pharmacology, chemical and [[biomolecular engineering]], and materials science at [[Vanderbilt University]]. She is a joint faculty member at [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]] in the Materials Science and Technology Division and the director of the [https://www.vanderbilt.edu/vinse/ Vanderbilt Institute of Nanoscale Science and Engineering].

Rosenthal is a researcher in the field of [[nanoscience]] and [[nanomaterials]], most notably [[quantum dots]] and [[nanoclusters]]. She is the leader of a highly interdisciplinary research team<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://my.vanderbilt.edu/rosenthalresearch/|title=Home|website=Vanderbilt University|language=en|access-date=2019-05-05}}</ref> based at Vanderbilt University which is focused on endeavors that span the fundamental study of quantum dots at the atomic scale to the development of designer nanomaterials for applications in diverse research areas ranging from solid-state lighting to biological imaging. A major focus of Rosenthal's current research is "to develop and use [[nanotechnology]] to elucidate molecular mechanisms of mental illness".<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Single quantum dot tracking illuminates neuroscience at the nanoscale|pages=741–752|journal=Chemical Physics Letters|volume=706|doi=10.1016/j.cplett.2018.06.019|date=2018-08-16|bibcode=2018CPL...706..741K|last1=Kovtun|first1=Oleg|last2=Tomlinson|first2=Ian D.|last3=Bailey|first3=Danielle M.|last4=Thal|first4=Lucas B.|last5=Ross|first5=Emily J.|last6=Harris|first6=Lauren|last7=Frankland|first7=Michael P.|last8=Ferguson|first8=Riley S.|last9=Glaser|first9=Zachary|last10=Greer|first10=Jonathan|last11=Rosenthal|first11=Sandra J.|pmid=30270931|pmc=6157616}}</ref>

==Education, career, and service==
Rosenthal received her B.S. with Honors in the field of Chemistry from [[Valparaiso University]] (1987).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.valpo.edu/college-of-arts-and-sciences/about/national-council/|title=National Council {{!}} College of Arts & Sciences|website=www.valpo.edu|access-date=2019-05-06}}</ref> Rosenthal played 4 years of Division 1 basketball for [[Valparaiso University]] while receiving her undergraduate degree.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Single quantum dot tracking illuminates neuroscience at the nanoscale|pages=741–752|journal=Chemical Physics Letters|volume=706|doi=10.1016/j.cplett.2018.06.019|date=2018-08-16|bibcode=2018CPL...706..741K|last1=Kovtun|first1=Oleg|last2=Tomlinson|first2=Ian D.|last3=Bailey|first3=Danielle M.|last4=Thal|first4=Lucas B.|last5=Ross|first5=Emily J.|last6=Harris|first6=Lauren|last7=Frankland|first7=Michael P.|last8=Ferguson|first8=Riley S.|last9=Glaser|first9=Zachary|last10=Greer|first10=Jonathan|last11=Rosenthal|first11=Sandra J.|pmid=30270931|pmc=6157616}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://cdn.streamlinetechnologies.com/valpoathletics/59633BB4-8F1E-4038-B89F-578D1639073E/WBBAllTimeRoster032119.pdf|title=Women's Basketball All-Time Roster}}</ref>

She went on to receive her Ph.D. in chemistry from the [[University of Chicago]] with [[Graham Fleming]] where her thesis was on "Femtosecond solvent dynamics: observation of the inertial contribution to the solvent response" (1993).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=17154819021509575466&hl=en&oi=scholarr|title=Google Scholar|website=scholar.google.com|access-date=2019-05-05}}</ref>
From 1993–1995, Rosenthal was a [[National Science Foundation]] Postdoctoral Fellow at [[Lawrence Berkeley National Lab]] and [[UC Berkeley]] where she worked with [[Paul Alivisatos]] and [[Charles Shank]]. During her time as a postdoctoral fellow, Rosenthal began her involvement with spectroscopic studies<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Rosenthal|first1=S. J.|last2=Yeh|first2=A. T.|last3=Alivisatos|first3=A. P.|last4=Shank|first4=C. V.|chapter=Size Dependent Absorption Anisotropy Measurements of CdSe Nanocrystals: Symmetry Assignments for the Lowest Electronic States |date=1996|editor-last=Barbara|editor-first=Paul F.|editor2-last=Fujimoto|editor2-first=James G.|editor3-last=Knox|editor3-first=Wayne H.|editor4-last=Zinth|editor4-first=Wolfgang|title=Ultrafast Phenomena X|volume=62|series=Springer Series in Chemical Physics|language=en|publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg|pages=431–432|doi=10.1007/978-3-642-80314-7_188|isbn=9783642803147|s2cid=102435598 }}</ref> on [[quantum dots]]. In 1996, Rosenthal began her independent faculty position on the Chemistry faculty at [[Vanderbilt University]]. Her independent research career has continued to be distinguished by her studies on [[quantum dots]] and [[nanomaterials]].

At [[Vanderbilt University]], Rosenthal is the director of the [https://www.vanderbilt.edu/vinse/ <nowiki>Vanderbilt Institute of Nanoscale Science and Engineering</nowiki>] and has served in that role for the past 12 years. During her tenure, the program has grown from 24 to 55 faculty members who have been awarded more than $250 million in funding for [[nanoscience]] research at the university.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://engineering.vanderbilt.edu/news/2019/rosenthal-to-step-down-as-vinse-director-planning-for-institutes-future-begins/|title=Rosenthal to step down as VINSE director; planning for institute's future begins|website=Vanderbilt University|language=en|access-date=2019-05-05}}</ref> The efforts of the Institute have also served to benefit opportunities and access to education in the field [[nanoscience]] education at the level of both undergraduate and graduate studies at Vanderbilt. At her undergraduate alma mater [[Valparaiso University]], Rosenthal serves as a member of the Valparaiso University College of Arts and Sciences National Council.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.valpo.edu/college-of-arts-and-sciences/about/national-council/|title=National Council {{!}} College of Arts & Sciences|website=www.valpo.edu|access-date=2019-05-06}}</ref>

Rosenthal's independent research career has been largely focused on the development of nanomaterials for applications in the energy sciences and the biosciences. She has also notably been one of the earliest advocates and leaders in support of utilizing (and extending capabilities) in [[electron microscopy]] for the purpose of advancing understanding of structure-function relationships relevant to the design of [[nanomaterials]] towards targeted technological applications.
